texts.title: Bread After the Night Shift
texts.summary: A hospital cleaner and an old baker share a roll every morning, until the bakery suddenly closes.

parts: Rosa cleaned floors at the city hospital. Her [shift] started at ten at night. It ended at six in the morning.
After work, she always stopped at a small bakery. It was her [habit]. The baker was an old man. His name was Mr. Haddad.
Every morning, there was a warm roll for her on the [counter]. “For the night worker,” he said. He never let her pay.
At first, they were [strangers|stranger]. Then they started to talk. He told her about his fig tree. She told him about her son in college.
One Monday, the bakery was dark. The door was locked. On Tuesday and Wednesday, it was still closed.
Rosa was [worried]. She asked the woman at the flower shop next door. “Mr. Haddad is in the hospital,” the woman said. “His heart.”
It was Rosa’s hospital! That night, she went to work early. She found his room. He looked small and tired in the bed.
She put a roll on his table. “For the night patient,” she said. Mr. Haddad laughed.
Rosa visited him every night before her shift. Slowly, he began to [recover]. Three weeks later, the bakery opened again.
In the window there was a new sign. It said, “Fresh bread every morning. Thank you, Rosa.”
Rosa cleaned floors at the city hospital. Her [shift] started at ten at night and ended at six in the morning. When she walked home, the streets were gray and quiet.
On her way, she always stopped at a small bakery on Elm Street. It was her [habit]. The baker, Mr. Haddad, was an old man with flour on his glasses.
Every morning, a warm roll was waiting for her on the [counter]. “For the night worker,” he said, and he never let her pay.
At first, they were [strangers|stranger]. But slowly, they started to talk. He told her about the fig tree in his yard. She told him about her son, who was in college far away.

Rosa felt [worried]. She asked the woman at the flower shop next door. “Mr. Haddad is in the hospital,” the woman said. “It’s his heart.”
It was the city hospital. It was her hospital. That night, Rosa came to work early and found his room on the fourth floor. He looked small and tired in the big bed.
She put a roll from the cafeteria on his table. “For the night patient,” she said. Mr. Haddad laughed for the first time in days.

Rosa cleaned floors at the city hospital. Her [shift] began at ten at night and ended at six in the morning, when the sky was turning from black to gray and the first buses were starting their routes. By then her arms were heavy and her feet hurt, but she liked the walk home through the quiet streets.

Halfway home, on the corner of Elm Street, there was a small bakery with a green door. Stopping there had become a [habit] she didn’t even think about anymore. The baker, Mr. Haddad, was a small old man who always had flour on his glasses and a radio playing old songs in the back.
Every morning, a warm roll wrapped in paper was waiting for her on the [counter]. “For the night worker,” he would say. When she tried to pay, he waved her money away as if it were a fly.

At first, they were [strangers|stranger] who shared a few polite words. But mornings add up. Over the months, he told her about the fig tree in his yard that gave far too many figs, and about the city where he was born. She told him about her son, who was studying engineering at a college eight hours away and called her every Sunday.

Then, one Monday, the green door was locked and the windows were dark. Rosa stood there for a minute, holding her bag, feeling strange without the warm paper in her hand. On Tuesday the bakery was still closed. On Wednesday too.

Rosa grew more and more [worried]. On Wednesday, she stepped into the flower shop next door. The owner looked at her sadly. “Mr. Haddad is in the hospital,” she said. “It’s his heart. He has no family here.”
“Which hospital?” Rosa asked, but she already knew. There was only one in this part of the city. It was her hospital.

That night, she came to work an hour early and asked at the front desk. She found him on the fourth floor, in a room at the end of a long hallway. He looked smaller than she remembered, lost in the white sheets, with a tube in his arm and nothing on his table.

Rosa took a roll out of her bag. It was from the hospital cafeteria, dry and a little sad. She set it on his table. “For the night patient,” she said. Mr. Haddad stared at her, and then he laughed so hard that a nurse looked in to check on him.

After that, Rosa visited him every night before her shift. She brought him the newspaper and told him what was happening on Elm Street. Slowly, he began to [recover]. Three weeks later, the green door was open again, and the smell of bread reached the corner before she did.
In the window, next to the price list, was a new sign written in careful letters: “Fresh bread every morning. Thank you, Rosa.” And on the counter, as always, a warm roll was waiting.

texts.title: Grandma’s Bread on the Screen
texts.summary: A woman far from home learns her grandmother’s bread over video calls.

parts: Leyla lived in a new country. She had a good job and nice friends. But on Sunday mornings, she was [homesick]. She missed her grandmother’s bread.
One Sunday, she called her grandmother on video. “Teach me your bread,” she said. Her grandmother laughed.
“Flour, water, salt and a little oil,” her grandmother said. “Those are the [ingredients|ingredient].”
“How much flour?” Leyla asked. “One cup? Two cups?” Her grandmother never [measured|measure] anything. She held up her hand. “A [handful]. Then another.”
Leyla mixed everything. Then she [kneaded|knead] the [dough]. She pushed it again and again. Her arms hurt. “Harder!” said her grandmother on the screen.
The first bread was flat and hard. Leyla almost cried.
“My first bread was worse,” her grandmother said. “Try again next Sunday.”
Leyla tried every Sunday. On the fifth Sunday, the bread was round, soft and warm. It smelled like her grandmother’s house.
Leyla held the bread up to the camera. Her grandmother clapped. Home did not feel so far away.
Leyla had lived in the new country for two years. She had a good job and kind friends, but on cold Sunday mornings she was still [homesick]. Most of all, she missed her grandmother’s bread.
So one Sunday, she called her grandmother on video. It was morning for Leyla and evening in the village. “Teach me how to make your bread,” Leyla said. Her grandmother laughed and put on her glasses.
“Flour, water, salt and a little oil,” her grandmother said. “Those are the only [ingredients|ingredient]. The rest is in your hands.”
Leyla had a measuring cup ready. “How much flour? One cup? Two?” Her grandmother never [measured|measure] anything. She held up her hand. “A [handful]. Then another. Then you feel it.”
Leyla leaned the phone against the sugar jar and started to mix.

Next, she had to [knead] the [dough]. She pushed it, folded it and pushed it again. After five minutes, her arms hurt. “Harder!” her grandmother said from the screen. “Use your shoulders, not just your fingers!”
An hour later, Leyla took the bread out of the oven. It was flat and hard, like a stone. She almost cried.
“My first bread was worse,” her grandmother said. “My mother gave it to the chickens. Try again next Sunday.”
Every Sunday for a month, Leyla called, and every Sunday the bread got a little better.
On the fifth Sunday, she pulled a round, golden loaf from the oven. She broke it open, and the warm smell filled her small kitchen. It smelled exactly like her grandmother’s house.
Leyla held the bread up to the camera. On the other side of the world, her grandmother clapped her hands. For the first time in a long time, home did not feel so far away.

Leyla had lived in the new country for two years. She had a steady job at a pharmacy, a small apartment with good light, and friends who invited her to dinner. Still, on gray Sunday mornings, she felt [homesick] in a way that was hard to explain. What she missed most was not a place but a smell: her grandmother’s bread, coming out of the oven while the whole house was still waking up.

So one Sunday, she called her grandmother on video. It was nine in the morning for Leyla and late afternoon in the village. Her grandmother’s face filled the screen, a little too close, the way it always did. “Teach me your bread,” Leyla said. Her grandmother laughed, went to find her glasses, and came back looking very serious.
“Flour, water, salt, a little oil,” she said, counting on her fingers. “Those are all the [ingredients|ingredient]. The rest is in your hands.”

Leyla had a measuring cup and a kitchen scale ready on the counter. “How much flour, exactly? One cup? Two?” But her grandmother had never [measured|measure] anything in her life. She held up one wrinkled hand. “A [handful]. Then another. Then you stop thinking and you feel it.”
Leyla leaned the phone against the sugar jar, rolled up her sleeves and began to mix.

Then came the hard part. She had to [knead] the [dough], pushing it away with the heels of her hands, folding it back, turning it, pushing again. After five minutes, her arms ached. “Harder!” her grandmother called from the screen. “Use your shoulders, not just your fingers! You’re petting it, not making bread!”
An hour later, Leyla opened the oven. The loaf was flat, pale and hard enough to knock on. She stared at it, and to her surprise, her eyes filled with tears.
Her grandmother only shrugged. “My first bread was worse,” she said. “My mother gave it to the chickens, and even the chickens complained. Call me next Sunday.”
So Leyla called the next Sunday, and the one after that. Each week, the bread was a little softer and a little rounder. Each week, they talked a little longer after it came out of the oven.

On the fifth Sunday, Leyla pulled out a round, golden loaf that sounded hollow when she tapped the bottom, just as her grandmother had taught her. She tore it open, and steam rose into the cold kitchen. The smell was exactly right.

She held the bread up to the camera. Thousands of miles away, her grandmother clapped her hands and called the neighbors to come and look. Leyla laughed, a piece of warm bread in her hand, and for the first time in a long time, home did not feel so far away.

texts.title: Learning to Drive at Forty
texts.summary: A mother who has never driven decides to get her license at forty.

parts: Amara was forty years old. She did not have a driver’s [license]. Every day, she took two buses to work. The trip took ninety minutes.
One night, she said, “I want to learn to drive.” Her daughter, Joy, was surprised. “Mom, you are forty!” “Yes,” said Amara. “And I am tired of buses.”
Her [instructor] was Mr. Lee. He was calm and kind. In the first lesson, Amara pushed the [brake] too hard. The car stopped very fast. “Gently,” said Mr. Lee. “Keep your hands [steady].”
Amara practiced every Saturday for three months. She learned to look in the [mirror] and to park.
Then she took the driving test. She was very nervous. She did not stop at a stop sign. She failed the test.
That night, Amara was sad. “I am too old,” she said. But Joy said, “You always tell me not to quit. So don’t quit.”
One month later, Amara took the test again. She drove slowly and carefully. She passed!
The next Monday, Amara drove to work. The trip took twenty minutes. She felt proud and [confident].
Amara was forty years old, and she had never driven a car. Every morning, she took two buses to her job at the hospital. The trip took ninety minutes each way, in rain, snow and summer heat.

One night at dinner, she made an announcement. “I’m going to get my driver’s [license].” Her daughter, Joy, who was seventeen, almost dropped her fork. “Mom, you’re forty!” “Yes,” Amara said. “And I’m tired of waiting for buses.”

Her driving [instructor], Mr. Lee, was a calm man with a soft voice. In the first lesson, Amara pressed the [brake] so hard that they both flew forward against their seat belts. “Gently,” Mr. Lee said, as if nothing had happened. “Keep your hands [steady]. The car will listen to you.”
Every Saturday for three months, she practiced. She learned to check her [mirror] before changing lanes, to park between two cars, and to stay calm when other drivers honked.
Then it was time for the test. Her hands were wet on the wheel. At the second corner, she forgot to stop completely at a stop sign. The test was over in ten minutes. She did not pass.
That night, Amara sat in the kitchen and said she was too old for this. Joy put her phone down. “You always tell me not to quit,” she said. “So don’t quit.”

A month later, Amara took the test again. This time, she drove slowly and carefully, and she stopped at every stop sign for a full three seconds. When it was over, the examiner smiled and said, “Congratulations.”

The next Monday, Amara drove herself to work. The trip took twenty minutes. She parked, turned off the engine and sat for a moment, feeling proud and [confident]. Then she called Joy. “I’m here,” she said. “And I’m early.”

Amara was forty years old, and she had never driven a car. In the town where she grew up, almost no one owned one, and in her first years in this country there had been no money and no time. So every morning, she took two buses to her job at the hospital: ninety minutes there and ninety minutes back, in freezing rain, in snow, in summer heat that made the bus windows sweat.

One night at dinner, she set down her spoon and made an announcement. “I’m going to get my driver’s [license].” Her daughter, Joy, who was seventeen, nearly choked on her rice. “Mom. You’re forty.” “I know how old I am,” Amara said. “I’m also tired of standing at bus stops.”

Her driving [instructor], Mr. Lee, was a calm, gray-haired man who spoke as softly as a librarian. In their first lesson, Amara stepped on the [brake] so hard that they both flew forward against their seat belts. Mr. Lee simply straightened his glasses. “Gently,” he said. “Keep your hands [steady]. The car will do what you ask. You only have to ask nicely.”

Every Saturday for three months, she practiced. She learned to check her [mirror] before every lane change, to squeeze into a parking space between two cars, and to keep breathing when a truck honked behind her. Some lessons went well. After others, she sat in the parking lot and wondered what she was doing.

Then came the test. Her palms were wet on the wheel before she even started the engine. At the second corner, trying to think about everything at once, she rolled through a stop sign without stopping completely. The examiner made a mark on his clipboard, and the test was over in ten minutes. She had failed.

That night, Amara sat at the kitchen table and announced that she was too old for this, that some people were simply not made for driving. Joy put down her phone, which was rare. “You always tell me not to quit when things get hard,” she said. “So don’t quit.” Amara had no answer for that, which was also rare.

A month later, she took the test again. This time she drove slowly and carefully, as if she were carrying a full cup of tea. She stopped at every stop sign and counted to three. When they pulled back into the lot, the examiner, the same man as before, looked up from his clipboard and smiled. “Congratulations,” he said.

The next Monday, Amara drove herself to work. The trip took twenty minutes. She pulled into the hospital parking lot, turned off the engine and sat for a moment in the quiet, feeling something she had not expected: not just proud, but [confident], as if a door she had thought was locked had been open the whole time. Then she called Joy. “I’m here,” she said. “And for once, I’m early.”

The head cook, Rosa, handed him a white [apron]. “Wash the dishes, cut the onions, and watch how we work,” she said. “Don’t worry about being fast. Fast comes later.”

Tomás started his new job at Casa Verde on a Friday, which everyone later told him was a terrible choice. Friday was the busiest night of the week. His [shift] began at four o’clock, but he arrived twenty minutes early and stood outside the back door, reading the same text message from the manager three times.

Inside, the head cook, a small woman named Rosa with flour on her sleeves, handed him a white [apron]. “Dishes first, then onions,” she said. “And watch how we move. Don’t try to be fast tonight. Fast comes later.”

By seven, every table in the dining room was full. The kitchen was hot, the fans roared, and orders flew over the noise in two languages. Tomás cut onions until his eyes streamed and his fingers smelled like them.

Then Rosa called his name. “Soup for table six. Bring the big pot to the front.” Tomás wanted to show that he could keep up, so he walked faster than he should have. He never saw the puddle near the sink.
His feet slid out from under him. The pot hit the tiles with a crash, and hot soup [spilled|spill] in a wide orange wave across the floor.

For a moment, the whole kitchen went silent. Even the fans seemed quieter. Tomás felt so [embarrassed] that he could not lift his eyes from the mess. He was certain that his first night would also be his last.
Rosa reached him first and helped him to his feet. “Are you burned?” she asked. He shook his head and started to apologize, but she held up a hand.
“My first day here, eleven years ago, I dropped a whole box of eggs,” she said. “Twenty-four eggs, all over the owner’s shoes. Now I run this kitchen.”

Somebody laughed, then somebody else, and the noise came back. Rosa’s story [encouraged|encourage] him more than any kind speech could have. He mopped the floor, washed his hands and went back to his onions. At midnight, as he hung up his apron, Rosa said simply, “See you tomorrow.” Tomás walked home with sore feet, feeling more [confident] than he had in months.

texts.title: How Does a Rainbow Form?
texts.summary: Sunlight is a mix of colors. Tiny raindrops bend the light and spread the colors apart, and we see a rainbow.

parts: After the rain, the sun comes out. Sometimes you see a rainbow in the sky. How does it happen?
Sunlight looks white. But it is really a [mix] of many colors: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet.
After rain, the air is full of tiny water [droplets|droplet]. Sunlight goes into each droplet. The light [bends|bend]. Each color bends a little differently, so the colors move apart.
Inside the droplet, the light hits the back and [reflects|reflect], like in a mirror. Then it comes out again. Now we can see each color.
A rainbow is a big [arc]. Red is on the outside. Violet is on the inside.
To see a rainbow, the sun must be behind you. The rain must be in front of you.
Sometimes you see two rainbows. The second one is [fainter|faint]. Its colors are in the opposite order.
You may see a rainbow when the sun comes out after rain, near a waterfall, or even in the spray of a garden hose. It looks almost like magic, but there is a simple reason for it.

Sunlight looks white, but it is really a [mix] of colors. You can see these colors in a rainbow: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet. Long ago, the scientist Isaac Newton used a piece of glass called a prism to show that white light can be split into these colors.
After rain, the air is full of tiny water [droplets|droplet]. When sunlight goes into a droplet, it [bends|bend] a little. Each color bends by a different amount, so the colors begin to spread apart.

The light then hits the back of the droplet and [reflects|reflect], almost like light in a mirror. As it comes out of the droplet, it bends again, and the colors spread out even more. Millions of droplets do this at the same time, and together they make a rainbow.

A rainbow is shaped like a big [arc], with red on the outside and violet on the inside. To see one, you must stand with the sun behind you and the rain in front of you. That is why rainbows are most common in the morning or late afternoon, when the sun is low in the sky.
Sometimes there is a second rainbow above the first. It is [fainter|faint], and its colors are in the opposite order. From an airplane, people can sometimes see a rainbow as a full circle.

A rainbow can appear when the sun breaks through after a storm, in the mist of a waterfall, or in the spray of a garden hose on a summer day. People have told stories about rainbows for thousands of years, but the science behind them is surprisingly simple.

Sunlight seems white, but it is actually a [mix] of all the colors we can see. In the 1660s, Isaac Newton passed sunlight through a glass prism and watched it spread into a band of colors: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet. He also showed that a second prism could bring the colors back together into white light.

Raindrops act like millions of tiny prisms. When a ray of sunlight enters a water [droplet], it slows down and [bends|bend]. Each color bends by a slightly different amount, violet the most and red the least, so the colors begin to separate.

The light then travels to the back of the droplet, where it [reflects|reflect] and heads back toward the front. As it leaves the droplet, it bends once more, spreading the colors even further apart. From where you stand, each droplet sends only one color toward your eye, so the rainbow you see is built from the light of millions of different drops.

Because of the angles involved, a rainbow always forms a curved [arc] around the point directly opposite the sun, with red on the outside edge and violet on the inside. You can only see one with the sun at your back and rain in front of you, and the sun must be fairly low, which is why rainbows are most often seen in the morning or late afternoon.

Sometimes a second, [fainter|faint] rainbow appears above the first. It forms when light reflects twice inside each droplet, and this reverses the order of its colors. Seen from an airplane, a rainbow can even form a complete circle. And because a rainbow depends on exactly where you stand, no two people ever see quite the same one.

texts.title: How Do Bees Make Honey?
texts.summary: Honey starts as a sweet liquid inside flowers. Thousands of bees work together to change it.

parts: Honey comes from bees. But bees do not find honey. They make it.
Bees live together in a [hive]. A big group of bees is called a [colony].
Bees fly to flowers. Many flowers have a sweet liquid inside. It is called [nectar]. A bee drinks the nectar. It keeps the nectar in a special stomach.
The bee flies back to the hive. It gives the nectar to other bees. They pass it from bee to bee. The nectar slowly changes.
Next, the bees put it in very small rooms made of [wax]. They move their wings fast, like fans. This dries the nectar. Now it is thick honey.
Then the bees [seal] each room with wax. The honey is food for the winter.
Bees also carry [pollen] from flower to flower. This helps plants make fruit and seeds.
Honey is one of the oldest sweet foods people eat. But where does it come from? Bees make it, and it takes a lot of teamwork.
Honeybees live together in a [hive]. One hive is home to a [colony] of thousands of bees. Each bee has a job.

Some bees fly out to find flowers. Inside many flowers is a sweet liquid called [nectar]. A bee drinks the nectar with its long tongue and keeps it in a special “honey stomach.” A bee may visit hundreds of flowers on one trip.
Back at the hive, the bee passes the nectar to younger bees. They pass it from mouth to mouth. Each time, the bees add natural chemicals that slowly change the nectar.

Next, the bees put the nectar into tiny six-sided rooms made of [wax]. Fresh nectar has a lot of water in it, so the bees beat their wings to move air over it. Slowly, the water dries up, and the nectar becomes thick, sticky honey.
When the honey is ready, the bees [seal] each room with a thin cap of wax. The colony will eat this honey in winter, when there are no flowers.
One bee makes only a tiny amount of honey in her whole life, much less than a spoonful. That is why a jar of honey needs the work of many thousands of bees.

Bees also help us in another way. As they move from flower to flower, they carry [pollen]. This helps plants make fruit and seeds. Many of the fruits and vegetables we eat need bees and other insects to grow.

People have been eating honey for thousands of years; ancient rock paintings even show people collecting it from wild bees. Yet few of us stop to think about how it is made. The answer is a remarkable example of teamwork.
Honeybees live in a [hive], where a single [colony] can contain tens of thousands of bees. Almost all of them are female worker bees, and each one has a job that changes as she gets older.

The older workers are the foragers. They fly out, sometimes several kilometers from home, in search of flowers. Deep inside many blossoms is a sugary liquid called [nectar]. A forager sucks it up through her long, tube-like tongue and stores it in a special honey stomach, separate from the stomach she uses for her own food. She may visit hundreds of flowers before she heads home.
At the hive, she passes the nectar to younger house bees, who pass it from one to another. Along the way, they add enzymes, natural chemicals that break the sugars in the nectar into simpler ones.

The bees then place the nectar into the honeycomb, a pattern of six-sided cells made of [wax] that the bees produce from their own bodies. Fresh nectar is mostly water, so the bees fan it with their wings, creating a steady flow of warm air. Over several days, much of the water dries up, and the nectar thickens into honey.
Once it is ready, the bees [seal] each cell with a thin wax cap. Stored this way, honey keeps for a very long time. It is the colony’s food supply for the winter, when there are no flowers to visit.
For all this effort, one worker bee produces only a tiny amount in her lifetime, a small fraction of a teaspoon. A single jar of honey is the life’s work of many thousands of bees.

Bees give us something even more valuable than honey, though. As they travel from blossom to blossom, grains of [pollen] stick to their hairy bodies and rub off on the next flower. This process, called pollination, helps many plants produce fruit and seeds, including many of the crops people depend on.

texts.title: How Does an Octopus Hide?
texts.summary: An octopus can change its color and its skin in less than a second, squeeze into tiny spaces, and shoot out ink.

parts: An octopus lives in the sea. It has eight arms and a soft body. Many animals want to eat it. These animals are [predators|predator].
An octopus has no bones and no shell. So how does it stay safe? It is very good at hiding.
Its skin can change color very fast, in less than one second. It can turn brown, red, gray, or white. It can look just like a rock. It can [blend in] with the sea floor. This is called [camouflage].
The skin can also change its [texture]. It can be smooth. Or it can become bumpy, like a rock.
An octopus can [squeeze] into very small holes, because its body is soft. The only hard part is its beak. The beak is in its mouth.
If a predator finds it, the octopus shoots out dark [ink]. The ink makes a cloud in the water. The predator cannot see. The octopus swims away fast.
The octopus is a sea animal with eight arms and a soft body. Sharks, eels, seals, and many big fish would like to eat it. These hunters are called [predators|predator].
An octopus has no shell and no bones to protect it, so it needs other ways to stay safe. Its best trick is hiding.

An octopus’s skin is full of tiny sacs of color. Small muscles open and close them, so the octopus can change its color in less than a second. It can turn brown, red, gray, or almost white, and it can even make patterns like spots and stripes. This helps it [blend in] with rocks, sand, and plants. Hiding like this is called [camouflage].

The octopus can also change the [texture] of its skin. It can make its skin smooth like sand or bumpy like a rock covered with sea plants. Then it is very hard to see, even when it is right in front of you.

Because it has no bones, an octopus can [squeeze] through very small openings. The only hard part of its body is its beak, a sharp mouth like a bird’s. If its beak can fit through a hole, the rest of its body can follow.

If a predator still finds it, the octopus has one more trick. It shoots out a cloud of dark [ink]. The predator cannot see through the cloud, and while it is confused, the octopus shoots away through the water.

With eight soft arms and no shell, the octopus might seem like an easy meal. Sharks, moray eels, seals, and large fish are all [predators|predator] that hunt it. Yet octopuses survive in oceans all over the world, largely because they are masters of disappearing.

Their most remarkable tool is their skin. It contains thousands of tiny, stretchy sacs filled with color, each one surrounded by muscles. When the muscles pull, a sac spreads open and its color shows; when they relax, it shrinks almost to nothing. Controlled by the octopus’s brain and nerves, these sacs can change its color and pattern in less than a second, letting it [blend in] with rock, sand, or coral. Scientists call this kind of disguise [camouflage].

Color is only half the trick. An octopus can also change the [texture] of its skin, raising small bumps and points so that it looks like a rough, weedy rock rather than an animal. Strangely, most octopuses are thought to be color-blind, and scientists are still working out how they match their surroundings so well.

An octopus has no bones at all. The only hard part of its body is its beak, which it uses to bite and eat. As a result, it can [squeeze] its soft body through a gap not much bigger than its beak, slipping into cracks where predators cannot follow.

When all else fails, it has one last defense. It squirts a cloud of dark [ink] into the water, which hides it and confuses the attacker. While the predator is distracted, the octopus pushes water out of its body like a jet and shoots away to safety.

texts.title: How Does the Moon Cause Tides?
texts.summary: The moon’s gravity pulls on the oceans. As the Earth turns, the sea rises and falls along the shore.

parts: At the beach, the sea moves. For a few hours, the water comes higher up on the sand. Then it goes back down. This is called the [tide].
Why does this happen? The answer is in the sky. It is the moon!
The moon has [gravity]. Gravity is a force. It [pulls|pull] things toward each other. The moon pulls on the Earth and on the ocean.
The ocean water moves toward the moon a little. On that side of the Earth, the water gets higher. The water also gets higher on the other side of the Earth.

The Earth turns around once every day. So at each beach, the water goes up and down. When the water at the [shore] [rises|rise], it is high tide. Most beaches have two high tides and two low tides every day.
The sun pulls on the ocean too. When the sun and the moon [line up], the tides are very big.

If you spend a day at the beach, you will see that the sea does not stay in the same place. For a few hours, the water slowly comes higher up the sand. Then, for a few hours, it moves back again. This rising and falling of the sea is called the [tide].
In most places, there are two high tides and two low tides about every 24 hours. But what makes the ocean move like this? The answer is the moon.

Everything in space has [gravity], a force that [pulls|pull] things toward each other. The Earth’s gravity keeps the moon going around us. At the same time, the moon’s gravity pulls on the Earth, and that includes the water in the oceans.

The moon’s pull makes the ocean water pile up a little on the side of the Earth that faces the moon. The water also piles up on the opposite side of the Earth. As the Earth turns, each beach passes through these two areas of high water. When a place moves into one, the water at the [shore] [rises|rise], and it is high tide. When it moves out, it is low tide.

The sun has gravity too, but it is very far away, so its pull on the oceans is smaller than the moon’s. When the sun, the moon, and the Earth [line up], at the new moon and the full moon, their pulls work together. Then high tides are higher and low tides are lower than usual.

In some places, the tide is very small. In others, it is huge. In the Bay of Fundy in Canada, the water at high tide can be more than 15 meters higher than at low tide. People who fish, sail, or walk along the coast always check the tide times.

Spend a whole day on the beach and you will watch the sea change. The water creeps slowly up the sand for about six hours, then slowly pulls back for about six hours more. This regular rising and falling of the sea is called the [tide], and in most coastal places it happens twice a day, arriving about fifty minutes later each day.
People noticed thousands of years ago that the tides seem to follow the moon. In the late 1600s, Isaac Newton explained why: it is a matter of [gravity].

Every object [pulls|pull] on every other object. The Earth’s gravity holds the moon in its path around us, and the moon’s gravity, in turn, tugs on the Earth. Solid ground hardly moves, but the oceans can flow, so the water on the side of the Earth facing the moon is pulled toward it and piles up slightly.

Surprisingly, a second pile of water forms on the far side of the Earth. There, the moon’s pull is weakest, so the Earth itself is pulled toward the moon a little more than that distant water is, and the water is, in effect, left behind. As the Earth spins, each stretch of coast passes through both areas of high water every day. As it does, the sea at the [shore] [rises|rise] to high tide, and in between it falls to low tide.

The sun also affects the tides, though less than half as strongly as the moon, because it is so much farther away. Twice a month, at the new moon and the full moon, the sun, moon, and Earth [line up]. Their pulls combine, producing extra-high and extra-low tides known as spring tides, a name that has nothing to do with the season. When the sun and moon pull at right angles, at the half moon, the tides are weaker.

The shape of the coast matters too. Out in the open ocean, the tide may raise the water by less than a meter, but in narrow bays it can be enormous. In Canada’s Bay of Fundy, the difference between high and low tide can be more than 15 meters, taller than a four-story building. For anyone who fishes, sails, or walks along the coast, knowing the tide times is not just useful; it can be a matter of safety.

texts.summary: A young man is annoyed by the notes his downstairs neighbor leaves, until the notes stop.

parts: Yusuf moved into a small apartment on the second floor. On his first night, he came home late. The front door was heavy, and it [slammed|slam] behind him.
In the morning, there was a note on his door. It said, “Please close the door softly at night. Thank you. — Mrs. Ortiz, 1B.”
Yusuf was [annoyed]. He did not even know her! He threw the note away.
But more notes came. “The trash goes out on Tuesday.” “Your box is with me.” They all had the same neat [handwriting].
Sometimes Yusuf saw Mrs. Ortiz in the [hallway]. She was small, with gray hair.
One day, Yusuf wrote a note back. He was [polite]. “Thank you for keeping my box. — Yusuf, 2B.” The next day, she wrote, “You’re welcome. You work too late. Eat something.”
After that, they wrote notes almost every day. Mrs. Ortiz told him about the buses. Yusuf told her about his job.
Then, for one week, there were no notes. Yusuf was worried. He knocked on her door.
Mrs. Ortiz opened it slowly. She was sick, and she lived alone. Yusuf understood. She was [lonely]. The notes were her way to talk to someone.
Yusuf brought her soup. The next day, he put a note on her door: “Call me if you need anything. I am right upstairs.”

When Yusuf moved into his first apartment in the city, he didn’t know anyone in the building. On his first night, he came home late from work. The front door was heavy, and it [slammed|slam] shut behind him.
The next morning, there was a note taped to his door. “Please close the door gently after 10 p.m. Some of us go to bed early. Thank you. — Mrs. Ortiz, 1B.”
Yusuf was [annoyed]. Why didn’t she just knock and tell him? He folded the note and threw it away.

But the notes kept coming. “Trash goes out on Tuesday night, not Wednesday.” “The mailman left your box with me.” “Watch the third step. It’s loose.” They were always written in the same neat, careful [handwriting].
Sometimes he saw Mrs. Ortiz in the [hallway]. She was a small woman with gray hair, and she always carried a bag of groceries.

One day, Yusuf decided to write back. He kept it short and [polite]: “Thank you for keeping my box. — Yusuf, 2B.” The next morning, a new note said, “You’re welcome. You work too late. Eat something.”
After that, they wrote to each other almost every day. She told him which bus was fastest. He told her about his new job and the town he came from.
Then, one week, there were no notes at all. Yusuf checked his door every morning. On the fifth day, he went downstairs and knocked.

Mrs. Ortiz opened the door slowly. She had been sick with the flu, and she had no family nearby. In the quiet apartment, Yusuf understood that she was [lonely]. The notes were her way of talking to someone.

That evening, he brought her soup from the corner store. The next morning, he taped a new note to her door: “If you need anything, call me. I’m right upstairs.” He wrote his phone number under his name.

When Yusuf moved into his first apartment in the city, he did not know a single person in the building, and he planned to keep it that way. He worked long hours at a warehouse across town and wanted nothing more than a quiet place to sleep. On his first night, he came home after eleven. The old front door was heavier than it looked, and it [slammed|slam] behind him with a bang that echoed up the stairs.
The next morning, a note was taped to his door at eye level. “Please close the front door gently after 10 p.m. Some of us go to bed early. Thank you. — Mrs. Ortiz, 1B.”
Yusuf read it twice and felt [annoyed]. If she had a problem, why couldn’t she just knock and say so? He crumpled the note and dropped it in the trash.

But the notes did not stop. “Trash goes out Tuesday night, not Wednesday.” “The mailman left your box with me. Knock anytime.” “Careful on the third step. It’s loose, and the landlord is slow.” Each one was written on the same small yellow paper, in neat, old-fashioned [handwriting] that leaned to the right.

Now and then he passed Mrs. Ortiz in the [hallway]: a tiny woman with silver hair, always carrying a grocery bag that looked too heavy for her. She nodded at him. He nodded back. Neither of them said a word.

Finally, mostly because he wanted his box, Yusuf wrote back. He kept it short and [polite]: “Thank you for keeping my package. — Yusuf, 2B.” The next morning, the reply was waiting: “You’re welcome. You come home too late. Eat something green.” He laughed out loud in the empty stairwell.

After that, the notes went back and forth almost every day. She told him which bus was fastest in the rain and which bakery sold yesterday’s bread for half price. He told her about the warehouse, and about the mountains outside the town where he grew up. Without quite noticing, he started to look forward to the yellow paper on his door.
Then, one week, there was nothing. Monday, no note. Tuesday, no note. By Friday, Yusuf could not stop thinking about the loose step and the heavy grocery bags. He went downstairs and knocked on 1B.

It took a long time for the door to open. Mrs. Ortiz stood there in a thick sweater, pale and coughing. She had been sick with the flu all week, and her only son lived three states away. Looking past her into the silent apartment, Yusuf finally understood. She was [lonely]. The notes had never really been about the door.

That evening, he brought her chicken soup and orange juice from the corner store. The next morning, he taped his own note to her door, on a piece of yellow paper she had given him: “If you need anything, call me. I’m right upstairs.” Under his name, he wrote his phone number, in his very best handwriting.

texts.title: Plot Seventeen
texts.summary: A man with no yard gets a small piece of a community garden, and his plants are not doing well.

parts: Farid was sixty-two. He lived in a small apartment. He had no yard.
When he was a boy, his father had a big garden. Farid missed the smell of tomatoes and mint.

Farid was sixty-two and lived in a small apartment on the fifth floor. He had a window, but no yard.

When he was a boy, his father had a big garden behind their house. Farid still remembered the smell of tomatoes and fresh mint in the summer. In his new country, he missed that smell more than he could say.
One spring, his name came up on the waiting list, and he got a [plot] in the community garden near the library. It was number seventeen, a small square of dirt between two paths.
Farid was excited. He bought twelve packets of [seeds|seed] and planted all of them in the [soil] in one afternoon, very close together. Then he watered them every morning and every evening.

Farid was sixty-two and lived in a small apartment on the fifth floor of a building with a broken elevator. He had one window that looked out at a parking lot, and on it he kept a single pot of basil that never seemed happy.

When he was a boy, his father had grown a big garden behind their house. Farid could still close his eyes and smell it: tomatoes warm from the sun, fresh mint, wet earth after the evening watering. In his new country, he had found work, an apartment and a few friends, but he had never found that smell again.

So when his name finally came up on the waiting list, after two years, he read the email three times. He had a [plot] in the community garden behind the public library. It was number seventeen, a small square of dirt between two gravel paths, and it was his.

Farid was so excited that he bought twelve packets of [seeds|seed] in one trip: tomatoes, cucumbers, beans, mint, eggplant and more. He planted all of them in the [soil] in a single afternoon, very close together, so that not one inch was wasted. Then he watered them every morning before work and every evening after.

The plot next to his, number eighteen, belonged to an older woman named Carmen. Her garden looked like a picture in a magazine. Her tomatoes were taller than she was, and her peppers were shiny and green. She nodded at him each morning, but she didn’t say much, and Farid was a little afraid of her.
By June, his own plants were short, pale and yellow. Some had already fallen over. He read about gardening on his phone at night, but the more he read, the less he understood what he was doing wrong.

One morning, Carmen stepped over the little wire fence between their plots without asking. She pushed her fingers deep into his soil, rubbed it between them, and shook her head. “Too much water,” she said. “And too close. Plants need space.” She tapped her chest. “And [patience].”

It was hard to hear, but Farid followed her [advice]. He watered every second day instead of twice a day. With a heavy heart, he pulled out half of the smaller plants so the others had room to breathe. For a week nothing happened. Then, slowly, the leaves turned green again.

By August, it was time to [harvest]. Farid had more cucumbers than he could eat in a year, and Carmen had a mountain of peppers she couldn’t give away fast enough. So they traded, a bag for a bag, and then another bag, and then a jar of her pickled peppers for a dish of his cucumber salad.

Now they talk every morning, in a mix of three languages. Carmen teaches him Spanish words, and he teaches her words in Farsi. Together, standing at the fence with dirt on their hands, they are learning the English names for everything that grows.

texts.title: The Story of the Bicycle
texts.summary: The first bicycle had no pedals. It took almost 70 years to get the bike we know today.

parts: The first bicycle was [invented|invent] in 1817 in Germany. A man named Karl Drais made it.
It was made of wood. It had two wheels but no [pedals|pedal]. You sat on it and pushed the ground with your feet.
You had to keep your [balance] on two wheels.
In the 1860s, people in France put pedals on the front wheel. But the ride was very bumpy.
Later, some bikes had a very big front wheel. They were fast, but people often fell off.
In 1885, a new bike came. Its two wheels were about the same size. A [chain] turned the back wheel. Soon bikes also had soft [tires|tire] filled with air.
The bicycle gave people [freedom]. They could travel far without a horse. Many women rode bikes to go places on their own.
Today, millions of people ride bicycles to work, to school or just for fun. But the first bicycle looked very different from the bikes we ride now.

It was [invented|invent] in 1817 by Karl Drais, a German inventor. It was made of wood and had two wheels, but no [pedals|pedal]. The rider sat on a seat and pushed against the ground with their feet, like walking or running. People called it a “running machine.” Riders learned to keep their [balance] on two wheels.

In the 1860s, people in France added pedals to the front wheel. Now riders could keep their feet off the ground. But the wheels were made of wood and iron, and the roads were rough, so the ride was very bumpy. Some people called these bikes “boneshakers.”

In the 1870s, a new kind of bike became popular. It had a huge front wheel and a tiny back wheel. A bigger wheel went farther with each turn of the pedals, so these bikes were fast. But the rider sat very high, and falls were common and dangerous.

In 1885, an English inventor named John Kemp Starley built a much safer bike. Its two wheels were about the same size, and the rider sat lower. The pedals turned a [chain], which turned the back wheel. Most bikes today still work this way.
A few years later, rubber [tires|tire] filled with air made riding much smoother and more comfortable.
By the 1890s, bicycles were everywhere. They cost less than a horse and were easier to take care of. For the first time, many working people could travel far from home on their own.
The bicycle brought a special kind of [freedom] to women. Many women rode bikes to work, to visit friends or to explore. Some even changed the way they dressed so they could ride more easily.

Today, the bicycle is so familiar that it is easy to forget it had to be [invented|invent] at all. Yet the bike we know took decades of experiments, and some of the early designs would surprise a modern rider.

The story usually begins in 1817 with Karl Drais, a German inventor. His machine had two wooden wheels, a seat and handlebars for steering, but no [pedals|pedal]. Riders moved by pushing against the ground with their feet, taking long, gliding steps. It was nicknamed the “running machine,” and it proved something important: a person could keep their [balance] on two wheels in a line, as long as they kept moving.

In the 1860s, French makers attached pedals directly to the front wheel. Riders could finally lift their feet off the ground, but the iron-rimmed wheels and rough roads made every trip a jolting experience, which is why many people called these machines “boneshakers.”

The 1870s brought the high-wheeler, often called the penny-farthing in Britain. Because the pedals were fixed to the front wheel, a larger wheel meant more distance with every turn, so designers made the front wheels enormous. These bikes were fast and fashionable, but riders sat high above the ground, and a small bump could throw them over the handlebars.

The real turning point came in 1885, when English inventor John Kemp Starley introduced the Rover. With two wheels of similar size and a lower seat, it was far safer. Instead of turning the front wheel directly, the pedals drove a [chain] connected to the back wheel, a design still used on most bicycles today.
A few years later, John Boyd Dunlop developed practical air-filled rubber [tires|tire]. Riding became smoother, faster and much more comfortable, and the modern bicycle was more or less complete.
The result was a bicycle boom in the 1890s. Bikes were cheaper to own than horses, and they let ordinary working people travel farther than ever before, on their own schedule.

For many women, the bicycle meant a new kind of [freedom]. They could go out alone, visit friends or explore the countryside without asking anyone for a ride. Long, heavy skirts were hard to ride in, so some women began wearing shorter skirts or loose trousers, a change that shocked some people at the time. More than a century later, the bicycle is still one of the simplest and most efficient ways to get around.

texts.title: The Story of the Postage Stamp
texts.summary: Long ago, the person who got a letter often had to pay for it. In 1840, a small stamp changed that.

parts: Long ago, sending a letter was hard. In some old empires, riders on horses carried messages. These [messengers|messenger] worked for kings, not for everyday people.

Later, many countries had a post office. But in Britain, letters cost a lot. The price depended on how far the letter went. Usually, the person who got the letter paid, not the [sender]. Sometimes people said no and did not take the letter.
A teacher named Rowland Hill had an idea. Make letters cheap. Make the price the same for every place in Britain. And the sender pays first.
In 1840, Britain made the first [stamp]. It was called the Penny Black. It cost one penny. It had a picture of Queen Victoria. People paid the [postage] and put the stamp on the letter.
Soon people sent many more letters. People started to use [envelopes|envelope]. Other countries made stamps too.
Today, some people collect stamps. A stamp [collector] may have thousands!
Today, you can send a letter almost anywhere in the world for a small price. But for most of history, it was not so easy.

Thousands of years ago, the kings of Persia and the rulers of Rome had riders who carried messages across their lands. These [messengers|messenger] changed horses at stations along the road, so the messages could travel fast. But this service was for the government, not for ordinary people.

Over time, many countries started a post office that everyone could use. But in Britain in the early 1800s, sending a letter was expensive and complicated. The price depended on how far the letter traveled and how many sheets of paper it had. Usually, the person who received the letter had to pay, not the [sender]. Some people could not pay, so they refused the letter, and the post office got no money.

A teacher named Rowland Hill had a better idea. He said there should be one low price for a letter going anywhere in Britain, and the sender should pay first. To show that the [postage] was paid, people would stick a small piece of paper on the letter.

In May 1840, Britain started selling the first [stamp] in the world that you could stick on a letter. It cost one penny and had a picture of young Queen Victoria. Because it was black, people called it the Penny Black.

The idea was a huge success. Sending letters became cheap, and people began writing many more of them. Because the price no longer depended on the number of sheets, people also started using [envelopes|envelope]. Soon other countries, like Brazil and the United States, made their own stamps.

Stamps also became something people love to collect. A stamp [collector] may keep thousands of stamps from all over the world. And even today, British stamps show a picture of the king or queen but not the name of the country, because Britain was the first.

Dropping a letter in a mailbox is one of the simplest things we do. Yet the system behind it, in which you pay a small, fixed price in advance and your letter can travel almost anywhere, is less than two hundred years old.

Long-distance messages are, of course, far older. About 2,500 years ago, the Persian Empire built a network of roads with stations where riders could change horses, allowing royal [messengers|messenger] to cross the empire in days rather than months. The Romans had a similar service. But these systems carried the government’s mail, not the letters of ordinary people.

By the early 1800s, Britain had a public post office, but using it was costly and confusing. Charges were based on the distance a letter traveled and the number of sheets of paper it contained, and the cost was usually paid by the person who received it rather than the [sender]. Many people simply refused letters they could not afford, leaving the post office with nothing for its trouble.

In 1837, a schoolteacher and reformer named Rowland Hill published a plan to fix the system. He argued for one low price, a single penny, for an ordinary letter going anywhere in Britain, paid in advance by the sender. As proof that the [postage] had been paid, the sender would attach a small printed label with glue on the back.

The government accepted the plan, and on 6 May 1840, the world’s first sticky postage [stamp], the Penny Black, could be used for the first time. It showed the young Queen Victoria’s head on a black background. The reform worked: letters became affordable for working families, and the number of letters sent across the country rose quickly.

There were other changes, too. Since the price no longer depended on the number of sheets, people began putting their letters in [envelopes|envelope], which soon became common. Other countries quickly copied the idea: Brazil issued stamps in 1843 and the United States in 1847.

Almost at once, stamps also became a hobby. Today a stamp [collector] may own thousands of stamps from around the world. And as a reminder of where it all began, British stamps still carry no country name, only a picture of the king or queen.

texts.title: The First Snow
texts.summary: A family from a warm country waits for their first winter, and the father worries about warm clothes.

parts: The Morales family came from Honduras. In Honduras, it is warm all year.
Now they lived in Ohio. It was December. Every morning, the children asked, “Will it snow today?”
Their father, Carlos, was worried. Winter coats were expensive. The children only had sneakers and thin jackets.
One Saturday, Sofi shouted, “Look!” Everything outside was white. It was their first snow.
Javier and Sofi ran to the door in their sneakers. “No!” said Carlos. “It is [freezing|freeze] out there!”
Then someone knocked. It was Mr. Bell, the old man next door. He had a big box. In the box were boots, hats, [mittens|mitten] and a red [sled].
“My grandchildren are grown up now,” he said. “You can [borrow] these.”
The children were [delighted]. They played in the snow all morning. Then Carlos went outside too. He began to [shiver], but he laughed and laughed.
The Morales family came from Honduras, where it is warm all year. Last summer, they moved to a small town in Ohio.
Now it was December. Every morning, Javier, who was nine, and Sofi, who was six, ran to the window and asked, “Will it snow today?”
Their father, Carlos, was worried. He had seen the prices of winter coats and boots at the store. The children only had sneakers and thin jackets, and he didn’t know how to pay for everything.
One Saturday morning, Sofi shouted, “Papá, look!” Everything outside was white: the cars, the trees, the street. It was their first snow.
Javier and Sofi ran to the door in their pajamas and sneakers. “No, no, no!” Carlos said. “It’s [freezing|freeze] out there!”
Just then, someone knocked. It was Mr. Bell, the old man who lived next door. He was holding a big cardboard box.

“I saw you didn’t have snow things yet,” Mr. Bell said. Inside the box were boots, wool hats, [mittens|mitten] and a red plastic [sled]. “My grandchildren are all grown up now. You can [borrow] these for the winter.”
The children were [delighted]. In ten minutes, they were outside, falling in the snow and pulling the sled up the little hill behind the house.
Carlos watched from the door. Then he put on his thin jacket and went out too. He began to [shiver] right away, but he caught a snowflake on his hand, and he laughed and laughed.
That night, he wrote a thank-you note to Mr. Bell. At the bottom, Sofi drew a picture of a red sled.

The Morales family came from Honduras, where the year has a wet season and a dry season but never a cold one. Last summer, they had moved to a small town in Ohio, because Carlos had found a job at a factory and his cousin lived nearby.

By December, the children could talk about nothing else. Every morning, Javier, who was nine, and Sofi, who was six, ran to the living room window before they even brushed their teeth. “Will it snow today?” they asked, pressing their noses to the cold glass. Their friends at school had told them about snowmen and snowball fights, and they had watched videos until they knew them by heart.

Their father did not share their excitement. Carlos had walked through the winter section of the department store, looked at the prices of coats and boots, and walked out again. His children had sneakers and thin jackets, and the rent and the electric bill came first. Every night he checked the weather on his phone and hoped the snow would wait until his next paycheck.
It didn’t wait. One Saturday morning in the middle of December, Sofi’s voice came from the living room, so loud that it woke the whole family. “Papá! Mamá! Look!”
Everything outside was white: the cars, the mailbox, the trees, the street. The world looked soft and quiet and new. It was their first snow.

Javier and Sofi ran for the front door, still in their pajamas and sneakers. “No, no, no!” Carlos said, catching Sofi by the back of her shirt. “It’s [freezing|freeze] out there! You’ll get sick!” Sofi’s face fell, and Javier looked at his father as if he had cancelled Christmas.

Just then, someone knocked. It was Mr. Bell, the old man from next door who waved from his porch every morning but rarely said more than hello. He was standing in the snow, holding a big cardboard box with both arms.

“I noticed you didn’t have any snow things yet,” Mr. Bell said, a little shy. Inside the box were boots in different sizes, wool hats, two pairs of [mittens|mitten] and a red plastic [sled] with a long rope. “My grandchildren are all grown up and live in Texas now. These were just sitting in my garage. You can [borrow] them for as long as you need.”

The children were [delighted]. Within ten minutes, they were outside in boots one size too big, falling backward into the snow, throwing it at each other, and pulling the sled up the little hill behind the house again and again.

Carlos watched from the doorway with Mr. Bell beside him. Then, because he could not stand it any longer, he put on his thin jacket and stepped outside. The cold hit him like a wall, and he began to [shiver] right away. But a snowflake landed on the back of his hand, perfect and white, and before it melted he started to laugh. He laughed until Sofi hit him with a snowball, and then he laughed even more.
That night, Carlos wrote a thank-you note to Mr. Bell, and he invited him for dinner on Sunday. At the bottom of the note, Sofi drew a red sled with four people on it, all of them smiling.

texts.summary: An eleven-year-old boy goes with his mother to the doctor to help with English, and it is harder than he thought.

Lucas translated every question, and his mother answered. So far, so good.

A calm voice began to speak Spanish from the phone. His mother asked question after question, more than she had ever asked a doctor before. Lucas just listened.

Lucas was eleven, and for most of his life he had been the English speaker in the family. His mother, Lucía, spoke Spanish at home and at work, and she knew only enough English to get through a short conversation, if the other person spoke slowly.

For weeks, she had been having bad headaches. She took pills from the store and kept working, until one evening Lucas found her sitting in the dark kitchen with her eyes closed. The next day, she made a doctor’s [appointment]. That night, she knocked on his door. “Will you come with me?” she asked. “You can [translate] for me.”
Lucas felt proud. He spoke English all day at school, he helped his mother at the grocery store and the bank, and he had once explained a phone bill to his uncle. This would be easy.

The office was small and very clean. The doctor, a woman with gray hair and red glasses, smiled at him as if he were a colleague, and began to ask about his mother’s [symptoms|symptom]. “How often are the headaches? Does light make them worse? Does she ever feel sick to her stomach?”
Lucas turned each question into Spanish, and his mother answered, and he turned the answers back into English. It felt a little like a game. So far, so good.

Then the doctor began to explain what she thought was happening. She talked about “blood pressure” and a “new medication” and “possible side effects.” Lucas knew these words in English, sort of, the way you know the faces of people you’ve never talked to. But he had no idea how to say them in Spanish. He opened his mouth, and nothing came out.

His face grew hot. He felt more [nervous] than he ever had before a test. What if he told her the wrong amount of medicine? What if he forgot something important? This wasn’t the grocery store or a phone bill. This was his mother’s health.
His mother saw his face. Without a word, she reached under the table and held his hand.

The doctor noticed too. She put her pen down. “We have an [interpreter] on the phone,” she said gently. “It’s free, and it’s their job. Would that help?” Lucas nodded so fast that his mother almost laughed.

A minute later, a calm voice began to speak Spanish through the phone on the desk. His mother sat up straighter. She asked question after question, more than Lucas had ever heard her ask a doctor, and she wrote the answers on a piece of paper. Lucas just sat beside her and listened.

Outside, in the parking lot, she pulled him into a long hug. “You were very [brave] in there,” she said. “But that was too much to put on you. Next time, I’ll ask for the interpreter myself.” She squeezed his hand. “You can just come and hold my hand.”

texts.summary: A tired man who needs money finds a wallet full of cash at a bus stop.

Daniel looked around. No one saw him. He was [tempted]. With this money, he could pay his rent.

A woman opened the door. Her eyes were red. “Are you Grace?” he asked. “I think this is yours.”
Grace was the [owner] of the wallet. She counted the money. It was all there. She laughed with [relief]. “This is my rent money,” she said.
She wanted to give him fifty dollars as a [reward]. “No, thank you,” Daniel said. “You need it more than I do.”
“You are very [honest],” Grace said. “Then come for dinner on Sunday.” On Sunday, Daniel ate with Grace and her daughter. He had no extra money, but he felt rich.
Daniel finished his shift at the car wash at six. His back hurt, and his rent was due on Friday. He was still eighty dollars short.
He sat down on the [bench] at the bus stop. That’s when he saw it: a black wallet, half hidden next to his leg. He opened it. Inside were three hundred dollars in cash.
Daniel looked around. The street was empty. Nobody had seen him.
He was [tempted]. With that money, he could pay his rent and buy groceries for two weeks. He thought about it for a long time.
Then he looked inside again. There was an ID card with a name and an address: Grace Mensah, 14 Hill Road. Behind the card was a photo of a little girl with a big smile.
Daniel’s bus came, and he let it go. He put the wallet in his pocket and started walking to Hill Road.
A woman opened the door. Her eyes were red, as if she had been crying. “Are you Grace Mensah?” Daniel asked. “I think this is yours.”

Grace was the [owner] of the wallet. She opened it and counted the money with shaking hands. All of it was there. She sat down on the step and laughed with [relief]. “This is our rent,” she said. “I thought it was gone.”
She tried to give him fifty dollars as a [reward], but Daniel shook his head. “You need it more than I do,” he said.

“You’re a very [honest] man,” Grace said. “Then at least come for dinner on Sunday.” That Sunday, Daniel ate rice and chicken with Grace and her daughter. He went home with no extra money, but he felt richer than he had in a long time.

Daniel finished his shift at the car wash a little after six. His back ached, his shoes were wet, and his phone had just reminded him, for the third time that day, that his rent was due on Friday. He was still eighty dollars short, and he had no idea where those eighty dollars would come from.

He dropped onto the [bench] at the bus stop and closed his eyes. When he opened them, he noticed something pressed against his leg: a black leather wallet, worn at the corners. He picked it up and looked inside. Three hundred dollars in twenties stared back at him.
Daniel looked up and down the street. A truck passed. A dog barked somewhere. No one was watching.

He would be lying if he said he wasn’t [tempted]. Three hundred dollars meant rent paid, with enough left over for groceries and maybe new shoes. He could tell himself the owner was probably rich. He could tell himself that anyone would do the same. He sat there with the wallet in his hand for a long time.
Then he looked again. Behind the cash was an ID card: Grace Mensah, 14 Hill Road. Behind that was a small photo of a girl about six years old, missing a front tooth and smiling with her whole face.
Daniel’s bus pulled up, opened its doors and waited. He let it go. He put the wallet in his jacket pocket and started walking toward Hill Road.

It took him twenty-five minutes to find the house. The woman who opened the door looked tired, and her eyes were red, as if she had been crying for a while. “Are you Grace Mensah?” Daniel asked. “I think this belongs to you.”

Grace was the [owner] of the wallet, and she stared at it as if it might disappear again. She counted the money with shaking hands. All of it was there. She sat down right on her front step and laughed, the kind of laugh that comes from pure [relief]. “This is our rent,” she said. “I’ve been looking for it since noon.”
She pressed a fifty-dollar bill into his hand as a [reward]. Daniel gave it back. “You need it more than I do,” he said, and found that he meant it.

Grace looked at him for a long moment. “You’re an [honest] man,” she said. “That’s not so common. If you won’t take money, then come for dinner on Sunday. My daughter will want to meet you.” That Sunday, Daniel sat at a crowded little table, eating rice and chicken while a six-year-old explained the rules of a game he did not understand. He walked home with exactly as much money as before, but he felt richer than he had in years.

Teodora lived alone on the third floor. She was sixty-eight, and she had lived in the building for five years. She knew her neighbors’ faces from the elevator, but not their names. Some evenings, she felt very [lonely].
In the dark, she found a [flashlight] in the kitchen drawer and lit a [candle] on the table.
Then she thought about her freezer. It was full of chicken, fish and the lamb she had bought for her birthday. Without power, all of it would [spoil] by morning.

Teodora took her flashlight and knocked on the door across the hall. A young couple with a baby opened it. Next, a tall man with a guitar. Then a student who was studying by phone light. Everyone had a freezer full of food that would spoil.

Together, they carried a small grill down to the [courtyard] behind the building. They cooked chicken, fish, lamb and vegetables. The student put candles on the picnic table, and the tall man played his guitar. For the first time, Teodora learned everyone’s names.
At eleven, the lights came back on. Everyone looked up at the bright windows and said, “Oh, no!” Then they all laughed.
The next month, there was a note in the hallway: “Courtyard dinner, Saturday at eight. Bring food. No power needed.”

It was one of those heavy July nights when the air feels like a wet towel, and the [storm] arrived all at once. The wind threw rain against the windows, thunder rolled over the roofs, and at exactly eight o’clock every light in the building went out with a soft click.

Teodora lived alone in apartment 3B. She was sixty-eight and had lived in the building for five years, ever since her husband died. She knew her neighbors’ faces from the elevator and the mailboxes. She knew which ones said good morning and which ones looked at their phones. But she didn’t know a single name, and on some evenings the quiet in her apartment felt so heavy that she turned on the television just to hear a voice. Those evenings, she felt very [lonely].

Now there was no television, no fan and no light. She felt her way to the kitchen, found a [flashlight] in the drawer by the sink, and lit a [candle] on the table. Its small flame made the room look like a different place.

Then she remembered the freezer. It was full: chicken, a big bag of shrimp, and a leg of lamb she had been saving for her birthday. In this heat, without power, all of it would [spoil] long before morning.
Teodora stood in the candlelight and did the math. One woman. Too much food. No way to keep it cold. She couldn’t possibly eat it all alone. But maybe, she thought, she didn’t have to.

She took her flashlight and knocked on the door across the hall before she could change her mind. A young couple opened it, the woman holding a baby who was fascinated by the flashlight. Down the hall, a tall man answered, with a guitar case by his door. At the end, a nursing student who had been studying by the light of her phone. Every single one of them had a freezer full of food and the same worried look.

So they carried a small grill down the stairs to the [courtyard] behind the building, where the rain had stopped and the air smelled clean. They cooked chicken and shrimp and lamb and the young couple’s vegetables, and someone brought out a bag of ice for the drinks. The student lined up candles along the picnic table. The tall man, whose name was Marcus, played old songs, and the baby fell asleep on Teodora’s shoulder. By ten o’clock, Teodora knew every name and two or three stories to go with each one.

At eleven, the lights came back on. All the windows above them lit up at once, bright and ordinary. Everyone looked up, and together, without planning it, they said, “Oh, no!” Then they laughed until the baby woke up.
A month later, there was a note taped to the wall in the hallway, in Teodora’s careful handwriting: “Courtyard dinner, Saturday at eight. Bring food. No power needed.”

texts.title: Why Do Leaves Change Color?
texts.summary: In fall, green leaves turn yellow, orange and red. Some of those colors were there all along.

parts: In summer, most leaves are green. In fall, many leaves turn yellow, orange or red. Why?
Leaves make food for the tree. They use sunlight to make sugar. The sugar gives the tree [energy].
A green [pigment] helps the leaves do this. A pigment is a color inside a plant.
In fall, the days get shorter and cooler. The tree stops making the green pigment. The green [fades|fade] away.
Now we can see yellow and orange. These colors were in the leaf all summer. They were [hidden] under the green.
Some trees also make new red colors in fall.
Then the leaves fall from the [branches|branch]. The tree rests in winter. This helps it [survive] the cold.
In many parts of the world, fall is a beautiful time of year. Trees that were green all summer turn bright yellow, orange and red. But why do leaves change color?

The answer starts with food. A leaf is like a small kitchen for the tree. It uses sunlight, water and air to make sugar, which gives the tree [energy]. To do this, leaves need a green [pigment] called chlorophyll. Leaves have so much of it that they look green.
When fall comes, the days get shorter and cooler. There is less sunlight, so the tree slowly stops making chlorophyll. The green color begins to [fade].
As the green goes away, other colors start to show. Yellow and orange pigments were in the leaf all summer, but they were [hidden] by the green. Now we can finally see them.
Red and purple are different. Some trees, like many maples, make new red pigments in the fall. Sunny days and cool nights help make these reds brighter.

Soon after, the leaves fall from the [branches|branch]. This does not mean the tree is dying. In winter, the ground can freeze, and it is hard for a tree to get water. By dropping its leaves, the tree saves water and energy. This helps it [survive] until spring, when new green leaves grow.

Every autumn, forests across much of North America, Europe and East Asia put on a spectacular show. Leaves that were green for months turn gold, orange, scarlet and purple, sometimes all on the same hillside. The change is more than beautiful; it is part of how trees get through the year.

To understand it, start with what a leaf does. Leaves are the tree’s food factories. Using sunlight, water and carbon dioxide from the air, they make sugar that gives the tree [energy]. This process depends on a green [pigment] called chlorophyll. During the growing season, leaves are packed with so much chlorophyll that its green covers every other color.

As autumn arrives, the nights grow longer and the air turns cooler. The tree responds by slowly shutting down its food production. It stops making new chlorophyll and breaks down what is left, and the green begins to [fade].
What remains are yellow and orange pigments, the same kind that give carrots their color. They were in the leaf all summer, [hidden] beneath the chlorophyll. Only now do they come into view.

The reds and purples have a different story. Trees such as many maples actually produce new red pigments in the fall. A run of sunny days and cool, but not freezing, nights tends to make these colors especially bright.

Eventually, a layer of special cells forms where each leaf’s stem meets the [branch], and the leaf breaks off. Losing its leaves might look like a loss, but for the tree it is a way to [survive]. In winter, frozen ground makes water hard to get, and broad leaves would lose a lot of water to the air. By dropping them, the tree saves water and energy and rests until spring, when a fresh set of green leaves appears.

texts.title: Why Is the Ocean Salty?
texts.summary: Rivers carry tiny bits of salt to the sea. The salt stays there, and over millions of years it adds up.

parts: Ocean water tastes very salty. River water does not. Why?
It starts with rain. Rain falls on rocks. Little by little, it breaks off very small bits of the rocks. Some of these bits are [minerals|mineral], like salt.
The salt [dissolves|dissolve] in the water. You cannot see it. Rivers carry it to the ocean.
The sun warms the ocean. Some of the water [evaporates|evaporate]. It goes up into the air. But the salt stays in the ocean.
This has happened for millions of years. So now the ocean has a lot of salt. If you took out all the salt, it could cover the land in a thick [layer].
Most rivers and lakes have [fresh water]. It has very little salt.
Do not drink ocean water. The salt makes you more [thirsty].
If you have ever swum in the ocean, you know the water tastes salty. But the rivers that flow into the ocean are not salty. So where does the salt come from?

The answer starts on land. Rain falls on rocks and soil. Over a long time, the rain slowly breaks down the rocks and picks up tiny bits of [minerals|mineral]. Salt is one of them. The salt [dissolves|dissolve] in the water, so you cannot see it.
Streams and rivers carry this water, with its tiny amount of salt, all the way to the ocean. River water has so little salt that we call it [fresh water].

At the ocean, the sun heats the water, and some of it [evaporates|evaporate]. The water goes up into the air and later falls again as rain. But the salt cannot go into the air. It stays behind in the ocean.
Some salt also comes from openings in the ocean floor, where hot water from deep inside the Earth comes up and brings minerals with it.

This has been happening for millions of years. Little by little, the salt has added up. Scientists say that if all the salt in the oceans were spread over the land, it would make a [layer] many meters thick.

Because of all this salt, people cannot drink ocean water. Your body has to use extra water to get rid of the salt, so salty water makes you even more [thirsty]. That is why sailors long ago had to carry fresh water on their ships.

Take a mouthful of seawater and you will not forget the taste. Yet the rivers that pour into the sea every day taste fresh. How can nearly salt-free water from the land end up in such a salty ocean? The answer is a slow process that has been going on for millions of years.

It begins with rain. As rain falls through the air, it picks up a little carbon dioxide, which makes it very slightly acidic. When it lands on rock and soil, it gradually breaks them down, releasing tiny amounts of [minerals|mineral]. Some of these are salts, and they [dissolve] completely in the water, which is why we cannot see them.
Rivers carry these dissolved minerals to the sea. The amounts are so small that we still call river water [fresh water], but every river is always delivering a little more salt to the ocean.

Once there, the salt is trapped. The sun heats the ocean’s surface, and water [evaporates|evaporate] into the air, eventually returning to the land as rain. The salt, however, cannot evaporate. It stays behind, and over time the ocean becomes far saltier than the water that feeds it.
Rivers are not the only source. On the ocean floor, openings called hydrothermal vents release hot water full of minerals from deep inside the Earth, and underwater volcanoes add more.

Most of the salt in the sea is the same kind we sprinkle on our food, and there is a huge amount of it. Scientists estimate that if it could all be removed and spread evenly over the land, it would form a [layer] many meters deep.

All that salt is why seawater is not safe to drink. To get rid of the extra salt, your kidneys have to use more water than the seawater gives you, so drinking it actually leaves you more [thirsty] and can make you seriously ill. For centuries, sailors surrounded by water had to carry fresh water on board.
