texts.title: Why Do We Get Hiccups?
texts.summary: A muscle under your lungs makes a sudden jump, and your throat snaps shut. That makes the “hic” sound.

parts: Hic! Hic! Almost everyone gets hiccups. But what are they?
Under your lungs, there is a big, flat [muscle]. It is called the [diaphragm]. It helps you breathe. Most of the time, it moves slowly and smoothly.
But sometimes it jumps. The jump is very [sudden]. Air rushes into your body. Then your throat closes fast. That makes the sound “hic.”
Why does this happen? Sometimes we eat too fast. Sometimes we drink soda. Sometimes we [swallow] too much air. Strong feelings, like excitement, can start hiccups too.
Most hiccups are [harmless]. They stop after a few minutes.
People try many [remedies|remedy]. Some people hold their breath. Some drink a glass of water slowly. These may help, but no one is sure. If hiccups last more than two days, see a doctor.
Almost everyone has had hiccups. They often start for no clear reason, and they can be funny or a little annoying. So what is really happening inside your body?

It starts with the [diaphragm]. This is a large, flat [muscle] under your lungs. When you breathe in, it moves down and pulls air into your lungs. When you breathe out, it moves back up. Usually, you do not even notice it.

A hiccup happens when the diaphragm makes a [sudden] jump that you cannot control. This pulls air quickly into your body. Less than a second later, your vocal cords close tightly, and the air stops. That is what makes the “hic” sound.

Hiccups can start when you eat or drink too fast, drink soda, or [swallow] a lot of air. Feeling excited or nervous can also start them. Even babies get hiccups, and they can have them before they are born.
Most hiccups are [harmless]. They usually go away on their own after a few minutes.

People around the world have their favorite [remedies|remedy]. Some people hold their breath. Others drink a glass of cold water in small sips or eat a spoon of sugar. Scientists have not proven that these tricks work, but they are safe to try. If your hiccups last for more than two days, it is a good idea to see a doctor.

Hiccups arrive without warning. One moment you are talking or laughing, and the next your body is making small, loud “hic” sounds that you cannot stop. Almost everyone gets them, yet few people stop to wonder what causes them.

The story begins with the [diaphragm], a large, dome-shaped [muscle] that sits under your lungs and separates your chest from your stomach. Each time you breathe in, it tightens and moves down, drawing air into your lungs. As you breathe out, it relaxes and rises again. It does this thousands of times a day, usually without you noticing at all.

A hiccup is a [sudden], uncontrolled tightening of the diaphragm, often together with the muscles between your ribs. It makes you pull in a quick breath. A split second later, the vocal cords in your throat snap shut and stop the air. That quick closing is what creates the familiar sound.

Common triggers include eating too quickly, drinking fizzy drinks, and [swallowing|swallow] air, which can stretch the stomach just below the diaphragm. Strong emotions, such as excitement or stress, can set them off too. Hiccups even happen before birth: babies often hiccup in the womb. Scientists are still not sure what purpose, if any, hiccups serve.
The good news is that ordinary hiccups are [harmless] and usually stop on their own within a few minutes.

Every culture seems to have its own [remedies|remedy]: holding your breath, sipping cold water slowly, or swallowing a spoonful of sugar. There is little scientific proof that any of them work, but they are generally safe, and simply waiting is often enough. Hiccups that last longer than two days are rare, and in that case it is wise to see a doctor.

texts.title: Why Do We Need Sleep?
texts.summary: Sleep is not wasted time. Your brain and body do important work at night.

parts: We sleep for about one third of our lives. Is this wasted time? No! Sleep is very important.
When you sleep, your body rests. But your brain stays busy.
Your brain sorts the things you learned that day. It puts the important things into your [memory].
Your body works at night too. Tired muscles get strong again. Small cuts [heal].
Sleep also helps your body fight [germs|germ].
Without enough sleep, it is hard to [focus]. You may feel sad or angry. Your [mood] gets worse.
Most adults need seven to nine hours of sleep. A bedtime [routine] can help. Go to bed at the same time every night. Put your phone away before bed.
Most people spend about one third of their lives asleep. That can sound like a lot of wasted time. But sleep is not wasted at all. While you sleep, your brain and body do important work.
Scientists are still learning about sleep, but they agree on one thing: we cannot live well without it.
Your brain stays busy all night. It sorts through the things that happened during the day. It keeps the important things and puts them into your [memory]. This is one reason sleep helps you learn.
People who sleep well after studying often remember more the next day.

Your body also uses the night to rest and grow strong again. Tired muscles get stronger, and cuts and other small injuries [heal]. Sleep also helps your body fight [germs|germ], so people who sleep too little may get sick more often.
When you do not get enough sleep, it is hard to [focus] on work or school. Small problems can feel big, and your [mood] can change quickly. Tired drivers are also more likely to have accidents.

Most adults need seven to nine hours of sleep each night. Children and teenagers need even more. A simple bedtime [routine] can help: go to bed at the same time every night, keep your room dark and cool, and put your phone away before bed.

The average person spends roughly a third of their life asleep. At first, that might seem like an enormous amount of lost time, hours that could be spent working, studying or with family. But scientists now know that sleep is anything but wasted. While your eyes are closed, your brain and body are busy with work they cannot do as well while you are awake.

One of the brain’s main jobs at night is sorting. During the day, it takes in a huge amount of information. During sleep, it replays some of it, keeps what seems important and stores it in long-term [memory], while letting much of the rest fade away.

This is why a good night’s sleep after studying often works better than staying up late. In many studies, people who slept after learning something new remembered it better than people who stayed awake.

Meanwhile, the body takes the chance to recover. Muscles rebuild after the day’s work, small injuries [heal], and the body releases hormones that help it grow. Sleep also supports the immune system, which protects you from [germs|germ]. This is one reason people who regularly sleep too little tend to catch colds more easily.

Missing sleep, even for a night or two, has clear effects. It becomes harder to [focus], make decisions and react quickly. Your [mood] suffers too: tired people often feel more irritable, worried or sad. Drowsy driving is a serious danger on the roads.

Most adults need seven to nine hours a night, and children and teenagers need more. Experts suggest a steady bedtime [routine]: going to bed and waking up at the same times, even on weekends, keeping the bedroom dark, quiet and cool, and putting screens away an hour or so before bed.

words.example: The trash **bin** is full.

words.meaning: The edge of the street, next to the sidewalk.
words.example: Put the bins at the **curb** on Sunday night.

words.meaning: A special day when many people do not work and offices are closed.
words.example: The bank is closed on the **holiday**.

words.meaning: The part of your mind that keeps what you have learned, seen or done.
words.example: She has a good **memory** for names.

words.meaning: To become healthy again after you are hurt or sick.
words.short: to get better after you are hurt
words.example: The cut on my hand **healed** in a week.

words.meaning: A very small living thing that can make you sick.
words.short: a tiny thing that makes you sick
words.example: Wash your hands to get rid of **germs**.

words.meaning: To give all your attention to one thing.
words.example: It is hard to **focus** when the room is loud.

words.meaning: How you feel at a certain time, like happy, sad or angry.
words.example: He is in a good **mood** today.

words.meaning: The things you usually do, in the same order, every day.
words.example: My morning **routine** is coffee, a shower, then the bus.

words.meaning: A home where a group of bees lives.
words.example: The farmer has ten bee **hives**.

words.meaning: A large group of the same kind of animal that lives together.
words.short: a big group of animals living together
words.example: A bee **colony** can have thousands of bees.

words.meaning: A sweet liquid inside flowers.
words.example: Bees drink **nectar** from flowers.

words.meaning: A soft material that bees make. Candles are often made of it.
words.example: This candle is made of **wax**.

words.meaning: To close something tightly so nothing can get in or out.
words.example: **Seal** the bag so the food stays fresh.

words.meaning: A fine yellow powder that flowers make.
words.example: **Pollen** in the spring makes me sneeze.

words.meaning: The power that lets living things move, grow and work.
words.example: A good breakfast gives me **energy** for the day.

words.meaning: A natural material that gives color to a plant, an animal or a thing.
words.example: Carrots get their orange color from a **pigment**.

words.meaning: To slowly become less bright or less strong.
words.example: The colors of my old shirt have **faded**.

words.meaning: Not easy to see or find.
words.example: The key was **hidden** under the mat.

words.meaning: A part of a tree that grows out from the trunk.
words.example: A bird sat on the **branch**.

words.meaning: To stay alive through a hard or dangerous time.
words.example: Some plants can **survive** with very little water.

words.meaning: To make or think of something new that did not exist before.
words.example: Who **invented** the telephone?

words.meaning: The part of a bike you push with your foot to make it go.
words.short: the part of a bike you push with your foot
words.example: Push the **pedals** to go faster.

words.meaning: Staying steady so that you do not fall.
words.example: I lost my **balance** on the ice.

words.meaning: A line of metal rings joined together.
words.example: The **chain** on my bike came off.

words.meaning: The rubber ring around a wheel. It is usually filled with air.
words.short: the rubber ring on a wheel
words.example: My bike has a flat **tire**.

words.meaning: Being able to do what you want and go where you want.
words.example: Her first car gave her more **freedom**.

words.meaning: A natural material found in rocks and soil, like salt or iron.
words.example: This water has a lot of **minerals** in it.

words.meaning: To mix into a liquid until you cannot see it.
words.short: to mix into a liquid and disappear
words.example: Sugar **dissolves** in hot tea.

words.meaning: When a liquid turns into a gas and goes into the air.
words.short: to turn into a gas and go into the air
words.example: The water in the pan **evaporated** in the hot sun.

words.meaning: Water that is not salty, like the water in rivers and most lakes.
words.example: Most lakes are full of **fresh water**.

words.meaning: An amount of something that covers a surface.
words.example: A **layer** of snow covered the cars.

words.meaning: Needing or wanting something to drink.
words.example: I am **thirsty** after the long walk.

words.meaning: A piece of cloth you wear over your clothes to keep them clean while you cook or work.
words.short: cloth worn to keep clothes clean
words.example: The cook put on a white **apron**.

words.meaning: When a liquid falls out of its container by accident.
words.short: to fall out by accident (a liquid)
words.example: I **spilled** coffee on my shirt.

words.meaning: Feeling bad or shy because other people saw you make a mistake.
words.short: feeling bad after a mistake in front of others
words.example: She was **embarrassed** when she called her teacher “Mom.”

words.meaning: To give someone hope or courage so they keep trying.
words.example: My friends **encouraged** me to take the class.

words.meaning: Sure that you can do something well.
words.example: After practice, he felt **confident** about the test.

words.meaning: To close very hard and with a loud noise.
words.example: Please don’t **slam** the door.

words.meaning: A little angry because something bothers you.
words.example: I was **annoyed** because the bus was late again.

words.meaning: The way a person writes letters with a pen or pencil.
words.short: the way someone writes by hand
words.example: My mother has beautiful **handwriting**.

words.meaning: A long, narrow space inside a building with doors to rooms or apartments.
words.short: a long space inside a building
words.example: Her apartment is at the end of the **hallway**.

words.meaning: Kind and respectful when you speak or write to people.
words.example: It is **polite** to say “please” and “thank you.”

words.meaning: Sad because you are alone or have no one to talk to.
words.example: He felt **lonely** in the big city.

words.meaning: Sad because you are far from your home and family and you miss them.
words.example: In her first year here, she was very **homesick**.

words.meaning: One of the foods you mix together to make a dish.
words.short: a food you use in a recipe
words.example: Eggs are an important **ingredient** in this cake.

words.meaning: To find out how much, how big or how long something is.
words.short: to find out how much or how big
words.example: **Measure** two cups of rice.

words.meaning: The amount you can hold in one hand.
words.short: as much as one hand holds
words.example: Add a **handful** of nuts to the salad.

words.meaning: To press, fold and push dough again and again with your hands.
words.example: **Knead** the dough for ten minutes.

words.meaning: A soft, thick mix of flour and water that you bake to make bread.
words.example: The **dough** must rest for one hour.

words.meaning: A long seat for two or more people, often outside.
words.example: We sat on a **bench** in the park.

words.meaning: Wanting to do something, even when you know it may be wrong or not good for you.
words.short: wanting to do something you shouldn’t
words.example: I was **tempted** to eat the whole cake.

words.meaning: The person something belongs to.
words.example: The **owner** of the dog came to get it.

words.meaning: The good, calm feeling when a worry or problem goes away.
words.short: the feeling when a worry ends
words.example: When the doctor said I was fine, I felt great **relief**.

words.meaning: Money or a gift you get for doing something good or helpful.
words.short: a gift for doing something good
words.example: She got a **reward** for finding the lost dog.

words.meaning: Telling the truth and not taking what is not yours.
words.example: He is an **honest** man. He never lies.

words.meaning: An official card or paper that says you are allowed to do something, like drive.
words.short: an official card that allows you to do something
words.example: You need a driver’s **license** to drive a car.

words.meaning: A person who teaches a skill, like driving or swimming.
words.short: a person who teaches a skill
words.example: My swimming **instructor** is very patient.

words.meaning: The part of a car you push with your foot to slow down or stop.
words.short: the part that stops a car
words.example: Press the **brake** at the red light.

words.meaning: Firm and not shaking or moving suddenly.
words.example: Hold the ladder **steady** for me.

words.meaning: A piece of glass that shows what is behind or in front of you. Cars have them so drivers can see behind them.
words.short: glass that shows a picture of you or what is behind
words.example: Look in the **mirror** before you change lanes.

words.meaning: Something you do often, almost without thinking about it.
words.example: Drinking tea after dinner is my **habit**.

words.meaning: A long, flat table in a store or kitchen where people pay, wait or prepare food.
words.short: a long table in a store or kitchen
words.example: Please put your bag on the **counter**.

words.meaning: A person you do not know.
words.example: A **stranger** helped me carry my bags.

words.meaning: Feeling afraid that something bad has happened or will happen.
words.example: My mother was **worried** when I came home late.

words.meaning: To get better and become healthy again after being sick or hurt.
words.short: to get better after being sick
words.example: It took me two weeks to **recover** from the flu.

words.meaning: A small piece of land, often used for a garden.
words.example: We grow beans in our **plot** at the community garden.

words.meaning: The small, hard part of a plant that you put in the ground to grow a new plant.
words.short: a small thing that grows into a plant
words.example: She planted tomato **seeds** in a pot.

words.meaning: The top part of the ground, where plants grow.
words.short: the earth that plants grow in
words.example: The **soil** in my garden is dark and wet.

words.meaning: Words that tell someone what you think they should do.
words.short: ideas about what someone should do
words.example: My friend gave me good **advice** about my new job.

words.meaning: To pick fruit, vegetables or other crops when they are ready.
words.short: to pick crops when they are ready
words.example: We **harvest** the apples in September.

words.meaning: To change words from one language into another language.
words.short: to change words into another language
words.example: Can you **translate** this letter into Spanish?

words.meaning: A sign that you are sick, like a fever, a cough or pain.
words.short: a sign that you are sick
words.example: A sore throat is a **symptom** of a cold.

words.meaning: A person whose job is to change what someone says into another language, while they are talking.
words.short: a person who changes speech into another language
words.example: The hospital has a free **interpreter** for patients.

words.meaning: Ready to do something hard or scary.
words.short: not afraid to do hard things
words.example: It was **brave** of you to speak in front of the class.

words.meaning: Very bad weather with strong wind and rain or snow.
words.example: The **storm** knocked down a tree on our street.

words.meaning: A small light that you hold in your hand. It uses batteries.
words.example: I keep a **flashlight** in the kitchen drawer.

words.meaning: A stick of wax with a string in the middle that you burn to make light.
words.short: wax that you burn for light
words.example: She lit a **candle** on the table.

words.meaning: When food spoils, it becomes old and bad, and you cannot eat it.
words.example: Milk will **spoil** if you leave it out of the fridge.

words.meaning: An open space outside, with walls or buildings around it.
words.example: The children play in the **courtyard** after school.

words.meaning: To become so cold that water turns into ice. “Freezing” means very, very cold.
words.short: to become very cold, or turn to ice
words.example: The lake will **freeze** in January.

words.meaning: A warm cover for your hand, with one part for your thumb and one part for your other fingers.
words.short: a warm glove with one part for the fingers
words.example: Put on your **mittens** before you go outside.

words.meaning: A small, flat thing you sit on to slide down a hill of snow.
words.short: something you ride down a snowy hill
words.example: The kids pulled the **sled** up the hill.

words.meaning: To take and use something that belongs to someone else, and give it back later.
words.short: to use something and give it back
words.example: Can I **borrow** your pen for a minute?

words.meaning: Very, very happy.
words.example: She was **delighted** with her birthday present.

words.meaning: When your body shakes a little because you are cold or afraid.
words.short: to shake because you are cold
words.example: I started to **shiver** at the bus stop.

words.meaning: A part of your body that tightens and relaxes to make you move.
words.short: a body part that helps you move
words.example: You use the **muscles** in your legs to walk.

words.meaning: A large, flat muscle under your lungs that helps you breathe.
words.short: a muscle that helps you breathe
words.example: When you breathe in, your **diaphragm** moves down.

words.meaning: Happening very quickly, when you do not expect it.
words.example: There was a **sudden** noise, and the baby woke up.

words.meaning: To make food, drink, or air go down your throat.
words.short: to make something go down your throat
words.example: Chew your food well before you **swallow** it.

words.meaning: Not able to hurt you or cause any problems.
words.short: safe; it will not hurt you
words.example: This spider is **harmless**, so you don’t need to be afraid.

words.meaning: Something you do or take to make a small health problem go away.
words.short: something that helps a problem go away
words.example: Hot tea with honey is my favorite **remedy** for a sore throat.

words.meaning: A very small drop of water or another liquid.
words.example: After the rain, there were **droplets** of water on the window.

words.meaning: To change direction and stop going straight, or to make something curved.
words.example: Light **bends** when it goes from air into water.

words.meaning: To send light or sound back from a surface, like a mirror does.
words.example: The lake **reflects** the trees, like a mirror.

words.meaning: A curved line, like part of a circle.
words.example: The ball flew through the air in a high **arc**.

words.meaning: Not strong or clear, so it is hard to see, hear, or smell.
words.short: not strong or clear; hard to see
words.example: We could see a **faint** light far away in the dark.

words.meaning: Different things put together.
words.example: The soup is a **mix** of rice, beans, and vegetables.

words.meaning: Colors or shapes that help an animal or a thing look like what is around it, so it is hard to see.
words.short: looking like the things around you to hide
words.example: The green color of the frog is good **camouflage** in the grass.

words.meaning: An animal that hunts and eats other animals.
words.short: an animal that hunts other animals
words.example: The lion is a **predator**.

words.meaning: How something feels when you touch it, like smooth, soft, or rough.
words.short: how something feels when you touch it
words.example: This bread has a soft **texture**.

words.meaning: To push yourself or something into a very small space.
words.short: to push into a small space
words.example: The cat **squeezed** under the door.

words.meaning: A dark liquid. Some sea animals shoot it out to hide. People also use it in pens.
words.example: My pen ran out of **ink**.

words.meaning: To look like the things around you, so people or animals do not notice you.
words.short: to look like what is around you
words.example: The brown rabbit **blends in** with the dry grass.

words.meaning: The rising and falling of the sea, which happens about two times a day.
words.short: the sea going up and down
words.example: At low **tide**, we walked far out on the sand.

words.meaning: The force that pulls things toward each other, like the force that makes things fall to the ground.
words.short: the force that pulls things down
words.example: Because of **gravity**, an apple falls from the tree to the ground.

words.meaning: To make something move toward you.
words.example: **Pull** the door to open it.

words.meaning: The land along the edge of the sea or a lake.
words.short: the land next to the sea or a lake
words.example: We sat on the **shore** and watched the boats.

words.meaning: To go up or become higher.
words.example: The river **rises** after a lot of rain.

words.meaning: To be in a straight line, one after the other.
words.short: to be in a straight line
words.example: The children **lined up** at the door.

words.meaning: A person who carries messages or letters from one person to another.
words.example: The king sent a **messenger** with the news.

words.meaning: The money you pay to send a letter or a package by mail.
words.example: How much is the **postage** for this package?

words.meaning: A small piece of paper you stick on a letter to show you paid to send it.
words.short: paper you put on a letter to mail it
words.example: I need a **stamp** for this birthday card.

words.meaning: The person who sends a letter, a package, or a message.
words.example: The **sender**’s address goes in the top left corner.

words.meaning: A paper cover that you put a letter or a card in before you mail it.
words.short: a paper cover for a letter
words.example: She put the letter in an **envelope** and wrote the address.

words.meaning: A person who keeps many things of one kind, like stamps or coins, as a hobby.
words.example: My uncle is a coin **collector**.

words.meaning: Late. It should have been returned or paid before now.
words.example: My library book is two days **overdue**.

words.meaning: Extra money you pay when you return or pay something late.
words.short: money you pay for being late
words.example: I paid the rent on time, so there was no **late fee**.

words.meaning: Your record with a bank, a library or a company. It shows your money, things or information.
words.short: your record with a bank or service
words.example: I checked my bank **account** on my phone.

words.meaning: A plastic card from your bank. When you pay with it, the money comes out of your bank account right away.
words.short: a bank card that uses your own money
words.example: She paid for the groceries with her **debit card**.

words.meaning: To make something start working, like a new card or phone.
words.example: Call this number to **activate** your new phone.

words.meaning: A secret number you use with a bank card. PIN means “personal identification number.”
words.short: a secret number for a card
words.example: Type your **PIN** to get cash from the ATM.

words.meaning: To come to an end. After that date, you can’t use it.
words.short: to stop being good to use
words.example: My driver’s license will **expire** next year.

words.meaning: When someone lies or tricks people to get their money or information.
words.example: The bank called to warn me about **fraud** on my card.

words.meaning: A meeting to talk about something. A parent-teacher conference is a meeting about a child at school.
words.example: I met my son’s teacher at the **conference**.

words.meaning: How much better someone is getting at something over time.
words.example: She is making good **progress** in English.

words.meaning: Free to meet or help at a certain time. It can also mean ready for you to get or use.
words.example: The doctor is **available** on Monday at 10:00.

words.meaning: To put your name on a list to do something or to get a time.
words.short: to put your name on a list
words.example: I will **sign up** for the swimming class.

words.meaning: A box or bag with something inside that is sent by mail or delivery.
words.example: A **package** came for you today.

words.meaning: Your name written in your own special way, to show you agree or got something.
words.example: Please put your **signature** at the bottom of the page.

words.meaning: One time that you try to do something.
words.example: He passed the test on his second **attempt**.

words.meaning: A number for a package. You use it online to see where the package is.
words.short: a number to follow a package
words.example: I typed the **tracking number** on the website.

words.meaning: A person who is just starting to learn something.
words.example: I am a **beginner** at the guitar.

words.meaning: At a high level. For people who already know a lot.
words.example: My sister takes an **advanced** math class.

words.meaning: A short test that shows which class or level is right for you.
words.short: a test to find your level
words.example: After the **placement test**, they put me in level 2.

words.meaning: When someone takes care of children while their parents work or study.
words.example: The school has **childcare** until 6:00 p.m.

words.meaning: To put your name on an official list so you can join a class or a program.
words.example: You can **register** for the class online.
